item.title: False sharing: two threads, one cache line
item.description:
Here's a puzzle. Two threads each increment their own counter 100 million times. They share no data, so they should scale perfectly. They don't.

#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>

constexpr long kIters = 100'000'000;

struct Packed {  // a and b share a cache line
    std::atomic<long> a{0};
    std::atomic<long> b{0};
};

struct Padded {  // a and b live on different cache lines
    alignas(128) std::atomic<long> a{0};
    alignas(128) std::atomic<long> b{0};
};

template <class Counters>
double seconds() {
    Counters c;
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::thread t1([&] { for (long i = 0; i < kIters; ++i) c.a.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); });
    std::thread t2([&] { for (long i = 0; i < kIters; ++i) c.b.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); });
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    return std::chrono::duration<double>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - start).count();
}

int main() {
    std::printf("packed: %.2fs\n", seconds<Packed>());
    std::printf("padded: %.2fs\n", seconds<Padded>());
}

On my Apple M3 (clang++ -O2, three runs):

packed: 0.73s
padded: 0.18s

The only difference is layout, and it makes the packed version 4× slower.

What's going on

Caches don't track individual bytes; they track lines. A line is the unit that moves between cores. When a core wants to write, the coherence protocol (MESI and its relatives) first needs that core to hold the line exclusively, which invalidates every other core's copy.

In Packed, a and b are 8 bytes apart, so they land in the same line. Each fetch_add on one core steals the line from the other core, and the line bounces back and forth for the whole run. The threads never touch the same variable, but the hardware sees them fighting over the same line. That's false sharing.

Padded puts each counter on its own line, so each core keeps its line in its own cache and never has to give it up.

How big is a cache line?

Usually 64 bytes on x86-64, but not always:

  • Apple M-series chips use 128-byte lines (sysctl hw.cachelinesize prints 128). With alignas(64) the two counters would still collide here, which is why the example uses 128.
  • C++17 added std::hardware_destructive_interference_size in <new> for this purpose. It's a compile-time guess, though. My clang reports 256 for AArch64 because it has to cover every ARM core it might run on, not just this one.

If you're shipping to a known machine (and in HFT you always are), check the real line size and pad with that.

Where this shows up

  • SPSC queues: the producer writes tail, the consumer writes head. Put them on the same line and every enqueue slows down the dequeuer.
  • Per-thread stats and counters: an std::array<Counter, N> indexed by thread id is a false-sharing machine unless each element is padded.
  • Thread-pool work items and anything else allocated back-to-back and written by different threads.

On Linux, perf c2c reports exactly which cache lines are contended between cores and which code is touching them.

Lesson: memory layout is part of your concurrency design. Two variables that are logically independent but physically adjacent are still shared.
